2.4.2. Extraction of the Pairs (Duka-atthuddhāra) 2.4.2.1.
Group on Causes (Hetu-gocchaka) 2.4.2.1.1.
The Pair on Causes (Hetu-duka)
Which phenomena are roots?
There are three wholesome roots, three unwholesome roots, and three indeterminate roots.
Non-greed is a wholesome root; non-hatred is a wholesome root; these arise in the wholesome states of the four planes.
Non-delusion (*amoha*), as a wholesome root, arises in the wholesome states of the four planes, excluding the four types of consciousness associated with knowledge that are of the sense-sphere.
Greed (*lobha*) arises in eight types of consciousness accompanied by greed.
Hatred (*dosa*) arises in two types of consciousness accompanied by displeasure.
Delusion arises in all unwholesome states.

Non-greed and non-hatred, as resultant causes (*vipākahetu*), arise in the resultant states of the four planes, excluding the rootless (*ahetuka*) consciousness-arising of the sense-sphere resultants.

Non-delusion, as a resultant cause, arises in the resultant states of the four planes, excluding the rootless consciousness-arising of the sense-sphere resultants and the four consciousness-arisings dissociated from knowledge (*ñāṇavippayutta*).

Non-greed (*alobha*) is a functional cause (*kiriyahetu*), and non-hatred (*adosa*) is a functional cause; excluding the rootless (*ahetuka*) consciousness-arising of the sense-sphere functional type, they arise in the functional consciousnesses of the three planes.

Non-delusion (*amoha*) is a functional cause; excluding the rootless consciousness-arising of the sense-sphere functional type and excluding the four consciousness-arisings dissociated from knowledge (*ñāṇavippayutta*), it arises in the functional consciousnesses of the three planes.
These phenomena are causes.
Which phenomena are not roots?

With the exception of the roots themselves, wholesome states in the four planes, unwholesome states, resultant states in the four planes, functional-ineffective states in the three planes, matter, and Nibbāna— these phenomena are not roots.
2.4.2.1.2. The Pair on With Cause (Sahetukaduka) Which phenomena are with cause?
With the exception of delusion accompanied by doubt and delusion accompanied by restlessness, the remainder of unwholesome states in the four planes [of existence].
Wholesome states; the resultant states of the four planes, excluding the rootless consciousness-arising that is resultant of the sense-sphere;
and the functional-indeterminate states of the three planes, excluding the rootless consciousness-arising that is functional of the sense-sphere—these states are with roots.

Which phenomena are rootless? Delusion accompanied by doubt, delusion accompanied by restlessness, the two sets of fivefold sense-consciousness, the three mind-elements, the five rootless mind-consciousness-elements, and both material form and Nibbāna— these phenomena are rootless.
2.4.2.1.3. The Dyad of Factors Associated with Roots (Hetusampayutta-duka) Which phenomena are associated with roots?
With the exception of delusion accompanied by doubt and delusion accompanied by restlessness, the remainder of unwholesome states in the four planes [of existence].
Wholesome states; the resultant states in the four planes, excluding the rootless consciousness-arising that is the result of sense-sphere consciousness;
and the functional-indeterminate states in the three planes, excluding the rootless consciousness-arising that is functional in the sense sphere—these states are associated with roots.
Which phenomena are dissociated from roots?
Delusion accompanied by doubt, delusion accompanied by restlessness, the two sets of fivefold sense-consciousness, the three mind-elements, the five rootless mind-consciousness-elements,
matter, and Nibbāna— these phenomena are dissociated from roots.
2.4.2.1.4. The Dyad of Roots and Rooted.
Which phenomena are both roots and rooted?
Those wherein two or three roots arise together.
These states are both causes and accompanied by a cause.
Which states are accompanied by a cause but are not themselves causes?
They are the wholesome and unwholesome states in the four planes, excluding the resultant mind-moments that are without cause in the sense-sphere realm.

In the four planes, [the states consisting of] resultant [consciousness], and the functional-inefficient consciousness of the sense-sphere— excluding the rootless (ahetuka) thought-arising— and the functional-inefficient (abyākata) consciousness of the three planes, excluding the roots arising therein:
these states are both with-root (sahetuka) and yet not roots (na hetū).
Rootless phenomena (ahetukā dhammā) should not be described as "both roots and associated with roots" (hetū ceva sahetukā ca), nor as "associated with roots but not roots" (sahetukā ceva na ca hetū).
2.4.2.1.5. The Dyad of Roots and Root-Associated.
Which phenomena are both roots and associated with roots?
Those states where two or three roots arise together—
these phenomena are both roots and associated with roots.
Which phenomena are associated with roots but are not themselves roots? They are:
wholesome and unwholesome states in the four planes; resultant states in the four planes, excluding the rootless mind-moments of the sense-sphere resultants;
and functional states in the three planes, excluding the rootless mind-moments of the sense-sphere functionals.
Inoperative indeterminate states; excluding those states that have arisen therein which are roots—these states are both associated with roots but are not themselves roots.
States dissociated from roots should not be said [to be either associated with roots or not].
[They may be] both causes and associated with causes, or [they may be] associated with causes but not causes themselves.
2.4.2.1.6. The Dyad of Non-causes with Causes:
Which phenomena are non-causes yet accompanied by causes?
In the four planes, there is the wholesome; the unwholesome; the resultant in the four planes, excluding the rootless (ahetuka) consciousness-arising of the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara);
and the functional-indeterminate (kiriyābyākata) in the three planes, excluding the rootless consciousness-arising of the sense-sphere and the roots arising therein.
These states are not roots, yet they are accompanied by roots.
Which states are not roots and are rootless?
The two sets of fivefold sense-consciousness, the three mind-elements, the five rootless mind-consciousness-elements, matter, and Nibbāna.
These phenomena are not roots; they are rootless.
Phenomena that are roots should not be described as "not roots and accompanied by roots," nor as "not roots and rootless."
2.4.2.2. Cūḷantaraduka 2.4.2.2.1.
Sappaccayaduka Which phenomena are with conditions?
Wholesome states in the four planes, unwholesome states, resultant states in the four planes, functional-inefficient states in the three planes, and all material form—
these phenomena are with conditions.
Which phenomena are without conditions?
Nibbāna—these are the phenomena that are without conditions.
2.4.2.2.2. The Dyad of the Conditioned (Saṅkhata-duka).
Which phenomena are conditioned?
Wholesome states in the four planes, unwholesome states, resultant states in the four planes, functional-inefficient states in the three planes,
and all form— these phenomena are conditioned.
Which phenomena are unconditioned?
Nibbāna—
these are the phenomena that are unconditioned.
2.4.2.2.3. The Pair on the Visible (Sanidassanaduka).
Which phenomena are visible?
The sense-sphere of form (rūpāyatana).
These phenomena are with visibility.
Which phenomena are without visibility?
The eye-base …pe… the tangible-object-base; wholesome [states] in the four planes, unwholesome [states] in the four planes …pe… [and so forth].

Resultant states, functional-ineffective states in the three planes, whatever form is non-demonstrable and non-reactive and included in the base of mental phenomena, and Nibbāna—these states are non-demonstrable.
2.4.2.2.4. The Dyad of With-Resistance (Sappaṭighaduka)
Which phenomena are with resistance?
The eye-base …pe… the tangible-object-base—
these phenomena are with resistance.
Which phenomena are non-reactive (appaṭigha)?

The wholesome and unwholesome states in the four planes; the resultant states in the four planes; the functional-undetermined states in the three planes; that form which is non-demonstrable and non-reactive and included within the base of mental objects (dhammāyatana);
and Nibbāna—these phenomena are non-reactive.
2.4.2.2.5. The Dyad of the Material.
Which phenomena are material?
The four great elements and the matter derived from the four great elements.
These phenomena are material.
Which phenomena are immaterial? They are:
wholesome states in the four planes, unwholesome states, resultant states in the four planes, functional indeterminate states in the three planes, and Nibbāna.
These phenomena are immaterial.
2.4.2.2.6. The Pair on the Mundane:
Which phenomena are mundane?
Wholesome states in the three planes, unwholesome states, resultant states in the three planes, functional-inefficient states in the three planes, and all form— these phenomena are mundane.
Which phenomena are supramundane?
The four paths that are not included [in the mundane world], the four fruits of recluseship, and Nibbāna—these states are supramundane.
2.4.2.2.7. The Dyad of "Cognizable by Someone" (Kenaci-viññeyya-duka).
All phenomena are cognizable by something; some are not cognizable by anything.
2.4.2.3. The Group on the Taints (Āsava-gocchaka). 2.4.2.3.1. The Dyad on the Taints (Āsava-duka).
Which phenomena are the taints?
There are four taints:
the taint of sensual desire, the taint of existence, the taint of views, and the taint of ignorance.

The taint of sensual desire arises in the eight types of consciousness accompanied by greed; the taint of existence arises in the four types of consciousness dissociated from views and accompanied by greed;
the taint of views arises in the four types of consciousness associated with views;
and the taint of ignorance arises in all unwholesome states.
These states are taints (āsava). Which states are not taints?

With the exception of the taints themselves, all remaining unwholesome states; wholesome states in the four planes; resultants in the four planes; functional-inefficients in the three planes; and form and Nibbāna.
These phenomena are without taints.
2.4.2.3.2. The Discourse on the Tainted:
Which phenomena are tainted?
Wholesome states in the three planes, unwholesome states, resultant states in the three planes, functional-inefficient states in the three planes, and all form—
these phenomena are with taints (*sāsava*).
Which phenomena are without taints (*anāsava*)?
The four paths that are not included [within the realms], the four fruits of recluseship, and Nibbāna—these states are without taints (anāsava).
2.4.2.3.3. The Dyad of States Associated with Taints (āsava-sampayutta-duka).
Which phenomena are associated with the taints (āsavas)?

The two types of unwholesome consciousness accompanied by mental grief, excluding the delusion arisen therein; and the remaining unwholesome states, excluding the delusion accompanied by doubt and the delusion accompanied by restlessness—these phenomena are associated with the taints.
Which phenomena are dissociated from the taints (āsavavippayutta)? They are:
the delusion (moha) arisen in the two types of consciousness accompanied by displeasure; the delusion accompanied by doubt; the delusion accompanied by restlessness;
the wholesome (kusala) in the four planes; the resultant (vipāka) in the four planes; and the functional-indeterminate (kriyā-abyākata) in the three planes.
Form and Nibbāna—these phenomena are dissociated from the taints (āsavavippayutta).
2.4.2.3.4. The Dyad of Taints and That Which Is Subject to Taints.
Which phenomena are both taints (*āsava*) and subject to taints (*sāsava*)?
Those very taints are both taints and subject to taints. Which phenomena are subject to taints but are not themselves taints?

Excluding the taints (*āsava*), the remaining unwholesome states, the wholesome states of the three planes, the resultant states of the three planes, the functional-inefficient states of the three planes, and all form (*rūpa*)—
these phenomena are both with taints and yet not themselves taints.
Phenomena that are without taints (*anāsava*) are not so described.
[There are things that are] both taints (*āsava*) and associated with taints;
[there are things that are] associated with taints but are not themselves taints. 2.4.2.3.5.
The Dyad of Taints and Association with Taints: Which phenomena are both taints and associated with taints?
Where two or three taints arise together—
these phenomena are both taints and associated with taints.
Which phenomena are associated with taints but are not themselves taints?
Excluding the taints, the remainder of unwholesome states—
these phenomena are associated with the taints but are not themselves taints.
Phenomena dissociated from the taints should not be described [in that way].
[There are things that] are both taints (*āsava*) and associated with taints; [there are things that] are associated with taints but are not themselves taints.
2.4.2.3.6. The Dyad of Being Dissociated from Taints yet Subject to Taints:
Which phenomena are dissociated from taints and subject to taints?
Delusion arisen in the two types of consciousness accompanied by displeasure; delusion accompanied by doubt; delusion accompanied by restlessness;
the wholesome in the three planes; the resultant in the three planes; the functional-indeterminate in the three planes;
and all form—these phenomena are dissociated from the taints but are subject to taints.
Which phenomena are dissociated from the taints and are without taints?
The four paths that are not included [within the mundane], the four fruits of recluseship, and Nibbāna—
these phenomena are dissociated from the taints and are without taints.
States associated with the taints (āsava) should not be described as either "dissociated from the taints and subject to the taints" or "dissociated from the taints and free from the taints.
2.4.2.4. The Group on Fettering (saññojana-gocchaka).
2.4.2.4.1. The Pair on Fetters (Saññojanaduka).
Which phenomena are fetters?
There are ten fetters: [list follows].
The fetter of sensual lust, the fetter of aversion, the fetter of conceit, the fetter of views, the fetter of doubt,
the fetter of adherence to rules and observances, the fetter of lust for existence, the fetter of envy, the fetter of avarice, and the fetter of ignorance.
The fetter of sensual lust arises in eight types of consciousness accompanied by greed.
The fetter of repulsion arises in two types of consciousness accompanied by displeasure.
The fetter of conceit arises in four types of consciousness associated with greed but dissociated from views.
The fetter of views arises in four types of consciousness associated with views.
The fetter of doubt arises in states of consciousness associated with doubt.
The fetter of adherence to rules and observances arises in four types of consciousness associated with wrong view.
The fetter of lust for existence arises in four types of consciousness associated with greed and dissociated from wrong view.
The fetter of envy and the fetter of avarice arise in two types of unwholesome states of consciousness accompanied by grief.
The fetter of ignorance arises in all unwholesome states.
These are the phenomena that are fetters.
Which phenomena are not fetters?

With the exception of the fetters themselves, the remaining unwholesome states, the wholesome states of the four planes, the resultant states of the four planes, the functional-indeterminate states of the three planes, matter, and Nibbāna— these phenomena are not fetters.
2.4.2.4.2. The Dyad of the Fetterable (Saññojaniyaduka) Which phenomena are fetterable?
Wholesome states in the three planes; unwholesome states; resultant states in the three planes; functional-inefficient states in the three planes; and all form.
These phenomena are subject to fetters.
Which phenomena are not subject to fetters?
The four paths that are not included [within the realms], the four fruits of recluseship, and Nibbāna.
These phenomena are not associated with the fetters.
2.4.2.4.3. The Dyad of Those Associated with the Fetters:
Which phenomena are associated with the fetters?
With the exception of restlessness-accompanied delusion, the remaining unwholesome states—
these are the phenomena associated with the fetters.
Which phenomena are dissociated from the fetters?

Delusion accompanied by restlessness, wholesome states in the four planes, resultant states in the four planes, functional-undetermined states in the three planes, matter, and Nibbāna—these phenomena are dissociated from the fetters.
2.4.2.4.4. The Dyad of Fetters and the Fetterable.
Which phenomena are both fetters and objects of fettering?
Those very fetters themselves are both fetters and objects of fettering.
Which phenomena are objects of fettering but are not fetters?

Excluding the fetters, the remaining unwholesome states, the wholesome states of the three planes, the resultants of the three planes, the functional-inefficients of the three planes, and all material form—
these phenomena are both objects of the fetters and are not themselves fetters.
Phenomena that are not objects of the fetters are not to be so described.
They are both fetters and objects of fettering; they are also objects of fettering but not fetters themselves.
2.4.2.4.5. The Dyad of Fetters and Association with Fetters:
Which phenomena are both fetters and associated with fetters?
Where two or three fetters arise together—
these phenomena are both fetters and associated with fetters.
Which phenomena are associated with fetters but are not themselves fetters?
Excluding the fetters, the remaining unwholesome states—
these phenomena are both associated with fetters and are not themselves fetters.
Phenomena dissociated from fetters should not be so described.
They are both fetters and associated with fetters; and they are associated with fetters but are not themselves fetters.
2.4.2.4.6. The Dyad of Factors Dissociated from Fetters but Subject to Fetters:
Which phenomena are dissociated from fetters yet subject to fetters?
Delusion accompanied by restlessness; the wholesome in the three planes; the resultant in the three planes; the functional-indeterminate in the three planes;
and all material form—these states are dissociated from the fetters but are subject to fettering.
Which states are dissociated from the fetters and are not subject to fettering?
The four paths that are not included [within the realms], the four fruits of recluseship, and Nibbāna—
these states are dissociated from the fetters and are not subject to fettering.
States associated with the fetters are not to be so described.
They are dissociated from the fetters and are subject to fettering; they are also dissociated from the fetters and are not subject to fettering.
2.4.2.5. Group on the Ties (Ganthagocchaka). 2.4.2.5.1.
The Dyad on the Ties (Ganthaduka).
Which phenomena are fetters?
There are four fetters:
the bodily fetter of covetousness, the bodily fetter of ill will, the bodily fetter of adherence to rules and observances, and the bodily fetter of dogmatic insistence that "this alone is the truth."
The bodily tie of covetousness arises in the eight types of consciousness accompanied by greed.
The bodily tie of ill will arises in the two types of consciousness accompanied by displeasure.
Both the bodily tie of adherence to rules and observances and the bodily tie of dogmatic insistence on "this alone is the truth" arise in the four types of consciousness associated with wrong view.
These states are fetters. Which states are not fetters?

With the exception of the fetters themselves, the remainder of unwholesome states; wholesome states in the four planes; resultant states in the four planes; functional-indeterminate states in the three planes; and form, as well as Nibbāna.
These phenomena are not fetters.
2.4.2.5.2. The Pair on the Fetterable:
Which phenomena are fetterable?
Wholesome states in the three planes, unwholesome states, resultant states in the three planes, functional-inefficient states in the three planes, and all material form—
these phenomena are subject to the ties.
Which phenomena are not subject to the ties?
The four paths that are not included [within the mundane], the four fruits of recluseship, and Nibbāna—these states are not subject to the ties.
2.4.2.5.3. The Dyad of States Associated with the Ties.
Which states are associated with the ties?
The four types of consciousness-arising associated with views; the four types of consciousness-arising accompanied by greed but dissociated from views, excluding the greed arisen therein;
the two types of consciousness-arising accompanied by displeasure, excluding the aversion arisen therein.
These states are associated with the ties (*gantha*).
Which states are dissociated from the ties?
The greed arisen in the four types of consciousness accompanied by greed and dissociated from the [four] views, and in the two types of consciousness accompanied by displeasure...
Among states of consciousness, resentment that has arisen, a state of consciousness accompanied by doubt, a state of consciousness accompanied by restlessness,
wholesome states in the four planes, resultant states in the four planes, functional-ineffective states in the three planes,
matter, and Nibbāna— these phenomena are dissociated from the ties.
2.4.2.5.4. The Dyad of Fetter and the Object of Fettering.
Which phenomena are both fetters and objects of fettering?
Those very fetters are both fetters and objects of fettering.
Which phenomena are both objects of the fetters and not themselves fetters?

With the exception of the fetters themselves, the remaining unwholesome states, the wholesome states of the three planes, the resultant states of the three planes, the functional-inefficient states of the three planes, and all form—
these phenomena are both objects of the fetters and not themselves fetters.
States that are not objects of the ties (aganthaniyā dhammā) are not to be described as either "both ties and objects of the ties" or "objects of the ties but not ties.
2.4.2.5.5. The Dyad of Ties and States Associated with Ties (Ganthaganthasampayuttaduka)
Which phenomena are both fetters and associated with fetters?
Those states wherein both wrong view and greed arise together—
these phenomena are both fetters and associated with fetters.
Which states are associated with the fetters but are not themselves fetters?
The eight types of consciousness accompanied by greed and the two types of consciousness accompanied by displeasure— with the exception of the fetters that have arisen therein—
these states are associated with the fetters but are not themselves fetters.
States dissociated from the ties (gantha) are not to be called "both ties and associated with the ties," nor are they to be called "associated with the ties but not ties.
2.4.2.5.6. The Dyad of States Dissociated from the Ties and Subject to the Ties.
Which states are dissociated from the ties but are objects of the ties?
The greed arisen in the four types of consciousness accompanied by greed and dissociated from the [four] views;
the aversion arisen in the two types of consciousness accompanied by displeasure; the type of consciousness accompanied by doubt; and the type of consciousness accompanied by restlessness.
Wholesome states in the three planes, resultant states in the three planes, functional-inefficient states in the three planes, and all material form—
these phenomena are dissociated from the ties but are subject to the ties.
Which phenomena are dissociated from the ties and not subject to the ties?
The four paths that are not included [in the mundane world], the four fruits of recluseship, and Nibbāna—
these states are dissociated from the ties and are not subject to being tied.
States associated with the ties are not to be so described.
Those dissociated from the fetters but subject to them; and those dissociated from the fetters and not subject to them.

2.4.2.8.2. The Pair on the Hindrance-Producing:
Which states are hindrance-producing?

Wholesome states in the three planes, unwholesome states, resultant states in the three planes, functional-inefficient states in the three planes, and all form— these phenomena are subject to hindrances.
Which phenomena are not subject to hindrances?
The four paths that are not included [in the mundane sphere], the four fruits of recluseship, and Nibbāna—these states are non-obstructive.
2.4.2.8.3. The Dyad on States Associated with the Hindrances.
Which phenomena are associated with the hindrances?
The twelve unwholesome types of consciousness—
these phenomena are associated with the hindrances.
Which phenomena are dissociated from the hindrances?
The wholesome in the four planes, the resultant in the four planes, the functional-indeterminate in the three planes, and matter and Nibbāna—
these phenomena are dissociated from the hindrances.
2.4.2.8.4. The Dyad of Hindrances and that which is Subject to Hindrance.
Which phenomena are both hindrances and subject to hindrance?
Those very hindrances themselves are both hindrances and subject to hindrance.
Which phenomena are obstructive but are not themselves obstructions?

With the exception of the obstructions themselves, all remaining unwholesome states; wholesome states in the three planes; resultant states in the three planes; functional-ineffective states in the three planes;
and all form—these phenomena are obstructive but are not themselves obstructions.
States that are not objects of the hindrances (anīvaraṇiya-dhammā) are not to be described as "both hindrances and objects of the hindrances," nor as "objects of the hindrances but not hindrances.
2.4.2.8.5. The Dyad of Hindrances and States Associated with Hindrances (Nīvaraṇa-nīvaraṇa-sampayutta-duka).
Which phenomena are both hindrances and associated with hindrances?
Those states where two or three hindrances arise together—
these phenomena are both hindrances and associated with hindrances.
Which phenomena are associated with the hindrances but are not themselves hindrances?
With the exception of the hindrances themselves, all remaining unwholesome phenomena—
these phenomena are associated with the hindrances but are not themselves hindrances.
States dissociated from the hindrances (nīvaraṇa) should not be described as "both hindrances and associated with hindrances," nor as "associated with hindrances but not hindrances.
2.4.2.8.6. The Dyad of States Dissociated from Hindrances but Subject to Hindrances (Nīvaraṇavippayutta-nīvaraṇiya-duka).
Which phenomena are dissociated from the hindrances but are subject to them?
Wholesome states in the three planes, resultant states in the three planes, functional-ineffective states in the three planes, and all form—
these phenomena are dissociated from the hindrances but are subject to them.
Which phenomena are dissociated from the hindrances and are not subject to hindrance?
The four paths that are not included [within the mundane], the four fruits of recluseship, and Nibbāna—
these phenomena are dissociated from the hindrances and are not subject to hindrance.

2.4.2.9. The Group on Misapprehension (Parāmāsa-gocchaka)
2.4.2.9.1. The Pair on Misapprehension (Parāmāsa-duka) Which phenomena are misapprehensions?
Misapprehension by view arises in those occurrences of consciousness associated with the four types of wrong views.
These phenomena are perversions (*parāmāsa*).
Which phenomena are not perversions?

With the exception of perversion itself, the remainder of unwholesome phenomena; wholesome phenomena in the four planes; resultant phenomena in the four planes; functional-ineffective phenomena in the three planes; and form and Nibbāna.
These phenomena are not misapprehensions.
2.4.2.9.2. The Dyad of Misapprehended Phenomena:
Which phenomena are misapprehended?
Wholesome states in the three planes, unwholesome states, resultant states in the three planes, functional-inefficient states in the three planes, and all matter—
these phenomena are the objects of misapprehension.
Which phenomena are not objects of misapprehension?
The four paths that are not included [within the mundane sphere], the four fruits of recluseship, and Nibbāna—these states are unclung-to.
2.4.2.9.3. The Dyad of States Associated with Clinging.
Which phenomena are associated with misapprehension (*parāmāsa*)?
The four types of consciousness-arising associated with views (*diṭṭhigata*), excluding the misapprehension arisen therein—
these phenomena are associated with misapprehension.
Which phenomena are dissociated from the perversions?
The four types of consciousness-arising accompanied by greed but dissociated from the modes of view; the two types of consciousness-arising accompanied by displeasure;
the consciousness-arising accompanied by doubt; the consciousness-arising accompanied by restlessness; and the wholesome states in the four planes.
Resultant states in the four planes, functional-undetermined states in the three planes, matter, and Nibbāna—
these phenomena are dissociated from the perversions.
Perversion itself is not to be so described.
[It is] both associated with misapprehension and dissociated from misapprehension.
2.4.2.9.4. The Dyad of Misapprehension and Misapprehended:
Which phenomena are both misapprehensions and misapprehended?
Thus, misapprehension is both misapprehension itself and that which is misapprehended.
Which phenomena are misapprehended but are not themselves misapprehensions?

With the exception of misapprehension itself, all remaining unwholesome states; wholesome states in the three planes; resultant states in the three planes; functional-ineffective states in the three planes; and all material form.
These phenomena are both objects of misapprehension and not themselves misapprehensions.

Phenomena that are not objects of misapprehension cannot be said to be "both misapprehensions and objects of misapprehension," nor can they be said to be "objects of misapprehension but not misapprehensions."

the four types of consciousness arising together with greed but dissociated from the modes of view (*diṭṭhigata*), and the two types of consciousness arising together with mental grief.
A state of consciousness accompanied by doubt, a state of consciousness accompanied by restlessness, wholesome states in the three planes,
resultant states in the three planes, functional-inefficient states in the three planes, and all matter—
these phenomena are dissociated from the perversions but are objects of perversion.
Which phenomena are dissociated from the perversions and are not adhered to?
The four paths that are not included [in the mundane], the four fruits of recluseship, and Nibbāna—
these phenomena are dissociated from the perversions and are not adhered to.

The Great Intermediate Dyads.
2.4.2.10.1. The Dyad with Object (Sārammaṇaduka) Which phenomena have an object?
Wholesome states in the four planes, unwholesome states, resultant states in the four planes, and functional-inefficient states in the three planes.
These phenomena have an object.
Which phenomena are without an object?
Material form and Nibbāna.
These phenomena are without an object.
2.4.2.10.2. The Dyad of Consciousness:
Which phenomena are consciousness?
Eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, the mind-element, and the mind-consciousness-element—
these states are consciousness.
Which states are not consciousness?
The aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, the aggregate of mental formations, material form, and Nibbāna—these phenomena are not consciousness.
2.4.2.10.3. The Dyad of Mental Factors (Cetasikaduka).
Which phenomena are mental factors?
The aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, and the aggregate of formations—
these phenomena are mental factors.
Which phenomena are non-mental factors?
Consciousness, matter, and Nibbāna—
these phenomena are non-mental factors.
2.4.2.10.4. The Couple of Factors Associated with Consciousness (Cittasampayuttaduka).
Which phenomena are associated with consciousness?
The aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, and the aggregate of mental formations.
These phenomena are associated with consciousness.
Which phenomena are dissociated from consciousness?
Matter and Nibbāna.
These states are dissociated from consciousness.
Consciousness itself should not be said to be either associated with consciousness or dissociated from consciousness.
2.4.2.10.5. The Pair on Conjoined with Mind (Cittasaṁsaṭṭhaduka).
Which phenomena are conjoined with mind?
The aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, and the aggregate of mental formations.
These states are conjoined with consciousness.
Which states are disjoined from consciousness?
Matter and Nibbāna.
These phenomena are dissociated from the mind.
The mind itself should not be said to be either associated with the mind or dissociated from the mind.
2.4.2.10.6. The Pair on Mind-Produced (Cittasamuṭṭhānaduka).
Which phenomena are mind-produced?

The aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, the aggregate of mental formations, bodily intimation, verbal intimation, and whatever other material form there is that is born of mind, caused by mind, and produced by mind.
The visible-form base, the sound base, the odor base, the flavor base, the tangible-base, the space element, the water element,
lightness of matter, malleability of matter, wieldiness of matter, integration of matter, continuity of matter, and physical nutriment—
these states are mind-originated.
Which phenomena are not mind-originated?
Consciousness itself, the remaining material phenomena, and Nibbāna—
these phenomena are not mind-originated.
2.4.2.10.7. Cittasahabhūduka:
Which phenomena are concomitant with consciousness?
The aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, the aggregate of mental formations, bodily intimation, and vocal intimation.
These phenomena are co-existent with consciousness.
Which phenomena are not co-existent with consciousness?
Consciousness itself, the remaining material form, and Nibbāna.
These phenomena do not coexist with the mind.
2.4.2.10.8. The Dyad of Phenomena that Follow the Mind:
Which phenomena follow the mind?
The aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, the aggregate of volitional formations, bodily intimation, and verbal intimation—
these phenomena are concomitants of the mind.
Which phenomena are not concomitants of the mind?
Mind and the remaining material phenomena, and Nibbāna—these states do not follow the mind.
2.4.2.10.9. The Dyad of States Conjoined with and Produced by Mind.
Which phenomena are conjoined with and produced by the mind?
The aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, and the aggregate of mental formations—
these phenomena are conjoined with and produced by the mind.
Which phenomena are not conjoined with and not produced by consciousness?
Consciousness itself, form, and Nibbāna—
these phenomena are not conjoined with and not produced by consciousness.
2.4.2.10.10. The Couple of Factors Conjoined with, Produced by, and Co-existent with Mind.
Which phenomena are conjoined with, produced by, and co-existent with mind?
The aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, and the aggregate of mental formations.
These phenomena are conjoined with, originated by, and co-existent with the mind.
Which phenomena are not conjoined with, originated by, and co-existent with the mind?
Mind, matter, and Nibbāna.
These states are not conjoined with, originated by, and co-existent with the mind.
2.4.2.10.11. The Dyad of States Conjoined With, Originated By, and Following After the Mind:
Which states are conjoined with, originated by, and following after the mind?
The aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, and the aggregate of mental formations—

Which phenomena are not conjoined with, originated by, and following along with the mind?
Mind, form, and Nibbāna—these phenomena are not conjoined with, produced by, or concomitant with mind.

The eye-base …pe… the mind-base—

The wholesome and unwholesome in the four planes; the resultants in the four planes; the functional-undetermined in the three planes; the four great elements; and Nibbāna.
These phenomena are not acquired by clinging.
2.4.2.10.14. The Dyad of Acquired Phenomena:
Which phenomena are acquired by clinging?
The result in the three planes and whatever form arises from the performance of karma—

Which phenomena are unacquired (anupādinnā)?

Wholesome states in the three planes; unwholesome states; functional-ineffective states in the three planes; and that form which is not produced by the performance of karma; the four paths that are not included [in the mundane]; the four fruits of recluseship; and Nibbāna—these phenomena are non-clung-to (anupādinnā).

Which phenomena are not subject to clinging?
The four paths that are not included [in the mundane world], the four fruits of recluseship, and Nibbāna—these states are not subject to clinging.

Which states are associated with clinging?

these states are associated with clinging.
Which phenomena are dissociated from clinging? They are:
the greed arisen in the four types of consciousness associated with lust but dissociated from the four views; the two types of consciousness accompanied by displeasure;
the type of consciousness accompanied by doubt; the type of consciousness accompanied by restlessness; and the wholesome [states] in the four planes.
In the four planes, resultant [states]; in the three planes, functional-indeterminate states, matter, and Nibbāna—these phenomena are dissociated from clinging.
2.4.2.11.4. The Dyad of Clinging and the Clingable.
Which phenomena are both clinging and objects of clinging?

Which phenomena are objects of clinging but are not clinging?

With the exception of clinging, all remaining unwholesome states, wholesome states in the three planes, resultant states in the three planes, functional-inefficient states in the three planes, and all matter—

2.4.2.11.5. The Dyad of Clinging and Association with Clinging:
Which phenomena are both clinging and associated with clinging?
Where view and greed arise together—

Which phenomena are associated with clinging but are not themselves clinging?
The eight types of consciousness accompanied by greed; with the exception of the clinging that has arisen therein—these states are both associated with clinging and are not themselves clinging.

Which states are dissociated from clinging and are not objects of clinging?
The four paths that are not included [in the mundane world], the four fruits of recluseship, and Nibbāna.
These states are dissociated from clinging and are not subject to clinging.
States associated with clinging should not be described as either "dissociated from clinging and subject to clinging" or "dissociated from clinging and not subject to clinging."
2.3.2.12. The Group on Defilements (Kilesagocchaka) 2.4.2.12.1.
The Dyad on Defilements (Kilesaduka) Which phenomena are defilements?
The ten bases of defilement (kilesavatthu) are:
greed, hatred, delusion, conceit, wrong view, doubt, sloth, restlessness, shamelessness, and fearlessness of wrongdoing.
Greed arises in the eight types of consciousness accompanied by greed.
Hatred arises in two types of consciousness accompanied by displeasure.
Delusion arises in all unwholesome states.
Conceit arises in four types of consciousness accompanied by greed and dissociated from wrong view.
View arises in those occurrences of consciousness associated with the four types of wrong view.
Doubt arises in those occurrences of consciousness accompanied by doubt.
Sloth arises in unwholesome states that are prompted by volitional effort.
Restlessness, lack of moral shame, and lack of moral dread arise in all unwholesome states—
these phenomena are defilements.
Which phenomena are not defilements?

Excluding the defilements, the remaining unwholesome states, the wholesome states of the four planes, the resultants of the four planes, the functional-undetermined states of the three planes, matter, and Nibbāna—these phenomena are not defilements.
2.4.2.12.2. The Dyad on States Subject to Defilement (Saṅkilesika-duka)
Which phenomena are subject to defilement?
The wholesome in the three planes, the unwholesome, the resultants in the three planes, the functional-indeterminate in the three planes, and all form—
these phenomena are subject to defilement.
Which phenomena are non-defiled?
The four paths that are not included [within the realms], the four fruits of recluseship, and Nibbāna—
these phenomena are non-defiled.
2.4.2.12.3. The Dyad of the Corrupt (Saṅkiliṭṭhaduka) Which phenomena are corrupt?
The twelve unwholesome types of consciousness.
These states are defiled.
Which states are undefiled?
The wholesome in the four planes, the resultants in the four planes, the functional-indeterminate in the three planes, and also form and Nibbāna.
These states are undefiled.
2.4.2.12.4. The Dyad of States Associated with Defilements:
Which states are associated with defilements?
The twelve unwholesome types of consciousness—
these phenomena are associated with defilements.
Which phenomena are dissociated from defilements?
Wholesome states in the four planes, resultant states in the four planes, functional-undetermined states in the three planes, matter, and Nibbāna—these phenomena are dissociated from the defilements.
2.4.2.12.5. The Dyad of Defiled Phenomena Associated with Defilements (Kilesa-saṅkilesika-duka)
Which phenomena are both defilements and subject to defilement?
Those very same defilements are both defilements and subject to defilement.
Which phenomena are subject to defilement but are not themselves defilements?

Excluding the defilements, the remaining unwholesome states, the wholesome states of the three planes, the resultant states of the three planes, the functional-inefficient states of the three planes, and all material form—
these phenomena are both subject to defilement and yet are not themselves defilements.
Phenomena that are not subject to defilement should not be said [to be defilements].
[There are things that] are both defilements and defiled; [there are things that] are defiled but are not defilements.
2.4.2.12.6. The Dyad of Defilements and the Defiled:
Which phenomena are both defilements and defiled?
Those same defilements are both defilements and defiled.
Which phenomena are defiled but not defilements?
With the exception of the defilements themselves, the remainder of unwholesome phenomena.
These states are both defiled and not themselves defilements.
States that are undefiled are not to be described as "both defilements and defiled," nor as "defiled but not defilements."
2.4.2.12.7. The Dyad of Defilements and Factors Associated with Defilements.
Which phenomena are both defilements and associated with defilements?
Those instances where two or three defilements arise together.
These states are both defilements and associated with defilements.
Which states are associated with defilements but are not themselves defilements?
With the exception of the defilements, the remainder of the unwholesome.
These states are both associated with defilements and are not themselves defilements.
States dissociated from defilements should not be described as either "both defilements and associated with defilements" or "associated with defilements but not themselves defilements."
2.4.2.12.8. The Dyad of Factors Dissociated from Defilements but Subject to Defilement (Kilesavippayutta-saṅkilesika-duka) Which phenomena are dissociated from defilements but subject to defilement?
They are: wholesome states in the three planes; resultant states in the three planes; functional-ineffective states in the three planes; and all form.
These phenomena are dissociated from the defilements yet subject to defilement.
Which phenomena are dissociated from the defilements and not subject to defilement?
The four paths that are not included [within the mundane], the four fruits of recluseship, and Nibbāna.
These states are dissociated from the defilements and are non-defiled.
States associated with the defilements should not be described as either "dissociated from the defilements and defiled" or "dissociated from the defilements and non-defiled."
2.4.2.13. Piṭṭhiduka 2.4.2.13.1. Dassanena-pahātabba-duka:
Which phenomena are to be abandoned by vision?
The four types of consciousness-arising associated with views, and the consciousness-arising accompanied by doubt—
these states are to be abandoned by vision.
The four types of consciousness-arising accompanied by greed but dissociated from views, and the two types of consciousness-arising accompanied by displeasure—
These phenomena may be abandoned by vision, or they may not be abandoned by vision.
Which phenomena are not to be abandoned by vision?

A state of consciousness accompanied by restlessness; wholesome states in the four planes; resultant states in the four planes; functional-ineffective states in the three planes; and material form and Nibbāna.
These phenomena are not to be abandoned by seeing.
2.4.2.13.2. The Pair on What is to be Abandoned by Cultivation:
Which phenomena are to be abandoned by cultivation?
A state of consciousness accompanied by restlessness—
these states are to be abandoned by cultivation.
Four types of state of consciousness accompanied by greed and dissociated from views, and two types of state of consciousness accompanied by grief—
These phenomena may be abandoned by cultivation, or they may not be abandoned by cultivation.
Which phenomena are not to be abandoned by cultivation?

The four types of consciousness-arising associated with views, consciousness-arising accompanied by doubt, wholesome states in the four planes, resultant states in the four planes, functional-ineffective states in the three planes, form, and Nibbāna.
These phenomena are not to be abandoned by cultivation.
2.4.2.13.3. The Dyad of Roots to be Abandoned by Seeing:
Which phenomena have roots that are to be abandoned by seeing?
The four types of consciousness associated with wrong view, and the type of consciousness accompanied by doubt— excluding the delusion arisen therein—
these states have roots that are to be abandoned by vision.

The four types of consciousness accompanied by greed but dissociated from wrong view, and the two types of consciousness accompanied by displeasure— these states have roots that are to be abandoned by cultivation.
These states may have roots that are to be abandoned by vision, or they may not have roots that are to be abandoned by vision.
Which states do not have roots that are to be abandoned by vision?

Delusion accompanied by doubt; the arising of consciousness accompanied by restlessness; the wholesome in the four planes; the resultant in the four planes; the functional-indeterminate in the three planes; and form and Nibbāna.
These phenomena do not have roots to be abandoned by vision.
2.4.2.13.4. The Dyad of Phenomena Having Roots to be Abandoned by Cultivation:
Which phenomena have roots to be abandoned by cultivation?
A state of consciousness accompanied by restlessness— with the exception of the delusion arisen therein—
these states have roots that are to be abandoned by cultivation.
Four types of state of consciousness accompanied by greed and dissociated from views, and two types of state of consciousness accompanied by displeasure.
These states may have roots to be abandoned by cultivation, or they may not have roots to be abandoned by cultivation.
Which states do not have roots to be abandoned by cultivation?
The four types of consciousness-arising associated with wrong view, consciousness-arising accompanied by doubt, and consciousness-arising accompanied by restlessness.
Delusion; wholesome states in the four planes; resultant states in the four planes; functional-undetermined states in the three planes;
and form and Nibbāna—these phenomena do not have roots to be abandoned by cultivation.
2.4.2.13.5. The Pair on With Initial Application (Savitakkaduka) Which states have initial application (*savitakka*)?

Wholesome states of the sense sphere, unwholesome states, and eleven types of consciousness-arising that are the resultants of wholesome states of the sense sphere, as well as [the resultants] of unwholesome states.
Two from the resultants, eleven from the functionals; the first fine-material-sphere jhāna from the wholesome, the resultant, and the functional;
and the supramundane first jhāna from the wholesome and the resultant—with the exception of the applied thought (vitakka) arisen therein—these states are "with applied thought" (savitakka).
Which states are without applied thought (*avitakka*)?
The two sets of fivefold sense-consciousnesses; the threefold and fourfold jhānas of the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*), whether wholesome, resultant, or functional;
the fourfold immaterial-sphere states (*arūpāvacara*), whether wholesome, resultant, or functional; and the threefold and fourfold supramundane jhānas (*lokuttara*).
Wholesome states and their results, applied thought, material form, and Nibbāna—these phenomena are without applied thought (*avitakka*).
2.4.2.13.6. The Pair on With Sustained Thought (*savicāra-duka*).
Which phenomena are accompanied by sustained application (*savicāra*)?
They are: wholesome states of the sense sphere; unwholesome states; eleven types of consciousness-arising that are the resultants of wholesome states of the sense sphere;
two types of resultant arising from the unwholesome; eleven types of functional arising; and the first jhāna of the fine-material sphere, both as wholesome and as resultant.
Excluding the vicāra arisen therein, these states— namely, the supramundane jhānas taken one by one, and those that are wholesome or resultant— are with vicāra.
Which states are without vicāra?
The two fivefold groups of consciousness; the fine-material-sphere jhānas of the triad [of roots] from the wholesome, the resultant, and the functional;
the four immaterial-sphere jhānas from the wholesome, the resultant, and the functional; the supramundane jhānas of the triad from the wholesome and the resultant;
sustained thought; matter; and Nibbāna.
These states are without investigation.
2.4.2.13.7. The Pair on With Rapture:
Which states are with rapture?
From the wholesome consciousness of the sense sphere (*kāmāvacara-kusala*), there are four types of consciousness accompanied by joy (*somanassasahagata-cittuppāda*); from the unwholesome, four;
from the resultants (*vipāka*) of the wholesome sense-sphere consciousness, five; from the functional (* kiriya*), five;

from the fine-material-sphere jhānas of the threefold set, both wholesome, resultant, and functional; and from the supramundane (*lokuttara*) jhānas of the threefold set, both wholesome and resultant—excluding the rapture (*pīti*) arisen therein.
These states are accompanied by zest.
Which states are without zest?

From the wholesome states of the sense sphere, there are four types of consciousness-arising accompanied by equanimity; from the unwholesome states, eight; and from the wholesome states of the sense sphere...
From the perspective of fruition (*vipāka*), there are eleven; from the fruition of the unwholesome (*akusala*), seven; from the perspective of functional (*kiriya*), six;
the fine-material-sphere pairs of jhānas are both wholesome, fruitional, and functional; the four immaterial-sphere jhānas are both wholesome, fruitional, and functional;
and the supramundane pairs of jhānas are both wholesome and fruitional, as well as zest (*pīti*), matter (*rūpa*), and Nibbāna.
These states are without rapture.
2.4.2.13.8. The Dyad of States Accompanied by Rapture:
Which states are accompanied by rapture?

From the wholesome states of the sense sphere (*kāmāvacara-kusala*), there are four types of consciousness-arising accompanied by joy (*somanassa-sahagata-cittuppāda*); from the unwholesome states (*akusala*), four;
from the fruition (*vipāka*) of the sense-sphere wholesome, five; from the functional (*kiriyā*), five;

from the wholesome, fruition, and functional jhānas of the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara-dukatika-jhāna*); and from the wholesome and fruition jhānas of the supramundane (*lokuttara-dukatika-jhāna*)—excluding the joy arising therein.
These states are accompanied by rapture (*pīti*).
Which states are not accompanied by rapture?

From among the wholesome states of the sense sphere (*kāmāvacara*), the four types of consciousness-arising accompanied by equanimity (*upekkhā*); from among the unwholesome states, eight; and from among the wholesome states of the sense sphere...
From the perspective of fruition (*vipāka*), there are eleven; from the fruition of the unwholesome (*akusala*), seven; from the perspective of functional (*kiriya*), six;
the fine-material-sphere pairs of jhānas from both the wholesome, the fruitional, and the functional; the four immaterial-sphere states from both the wholesome and the fruitional;
the supramundane pairs of jhānas from both the wholesome and the fruitional; and joy (*pīti*), material form (*rūpa*), and Nibbāna.
These states are not accompanied by rapture.
2.4.2.13.9. The Pair on Accompaniment by Pleasure:
Which states are accompanied by pleasure?
From the wholesome consciousness of the sense sphere (*kāmāvacara-kusala*), there are four types of consciousness accompanied by joy; from the unwholesome (*akusala*), four;
from the resultants (*vipāka*) of the wholesome sense-sphere consciousness, six; from the functional (* kiriya*), five;

the threefold and fourfold jhānas of the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*), both from the wholesome and the resultant; and the threefold and fourfold supramundane (*lokuttara*) jhānas, both from the wholesome and the resultant—excluding the pleasure (*sukha*) arising therein.
These states are accompanied by pleasure.
Which states are not accompanied by pleasure?
From the wholesome [states] of the sense sphere, four types of consciousness-arising accompanied by equanimity; from the unwholesome, eight; and from the wholesome of the sense sphere...

From the perspective of result (vipāka), there are ten; from the result of the unwholesome, seven; from the perspective of functional (kiriya), six; the fourth jhāna of the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara) is wholesome, resultant, and functional;
the four formless attainments (āruppa) are wholesome, resultant, and functional;
and the supramundane (lokuttara) fourth jhāna is wholesome and resultant—namely, pleasure, form, and Nibbāna.
These states are not accompanied by pleasure.
2.4.2.13.10. The Dyad of States Accompanied by Equanimity:
Which states are accompanied by equanimity?
From the wholesome of the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara), there are four types of consciousness-arising accompanied by equanimity; from the unwholesome, six;

from the resultant of the wholesome of the sense-sphere, ten; from the resultant of the unwholesome, six; from the functional (kiriyā), six; the fourth jhāna of the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara) from both the wholesome and the resultant;
and the four formless attainments (āruppa) from both the wholesome and the resultant, as well as the functional.
And the supramundane fourth jhāna, both as wholesome and as fruition— excluding the equanimity arisen therein—
these states are accompanied by equanimity.
Which states are not accompanied by equanimity?

From the wholesome consciousnesses of the sense sphere (*kāmāvacara-kusala*), there are four types of consciousness arising accompanied by joy (*somanassasahagata-cittuppāda*); from the unwholesome (*akusala*), six;
from the resultants (*vipāka*) of the wholesome of the sense sphere, six; from the resultant of the unwholesome, one; from the functional (*kiriya*), five;

from the wholesome, resultant, and functional states of the fine-material-sphere (*rūpāvacara*) first, second, third, and fourth jhānas; and from the wholesome and resultant states of the supramundane (*lokuttara*) first, second, third, and fourth jhānas.
Equanimity and form, and Nibbāna—these phenomena are not accompanied by equanimity.
2.4.2.13.11. The Dyad of the Sense-Sphere.

Which phenomena belong to the sense sphere (*kāmāvacara*)? Wholesome states of the sense sphere, unwholesome states, all resultants of the sense sphere, indeterminate functional states of the sense sphere, and all form (*rūpa*)—
these phenomena belong to the sense sphere.
Which phenomena are not of the sense sphere?
Those of the fine-material sphere, those of the immaterial sphere, and those that are unincluded—
these phenomena are not of the sense sphere.
2.4.2.13.12. The Pair on the Form-Sphere (Rūpāvacaraduka).
Which phenomena are of the form-sphere?
The fourfold and fivefold jhānas of the form-sphere, whether as wholesome, resultant, or functional.
These states belong to the fine-material sphere.
Which states do not belong to the fine-material sphere?
Those belonging to the sense-sphere, those belonging to the immaterial sphere, and those that are unincluded.
These states do not belong to the fine-material sphere (na rūpāvacarā).
2.4.2.13.13. The Pair on the Immaterial Sphere (Arūpāvacaraduka):
Which states belong to the immaterial sphere?
The four formless attainments, whether wholesome, resultant, or functional—
these states belong to the formless sphere.
Which states do not belong to the formless sphere?
Those states belonging to the sense sphere, those belonging to the fine-material sphere, and those that are unincluded—these states are not belonging to the immaterial sphere.
2.4.2.13.14. The Pair on the Included.
Which phenomena are included?
The wholesome in the three planes, the unwholesome, the resultants in the three planes, the functional-undetermined in the three planes,
and all form— these phenomena are included.
Which phenomena are not included within the realms?
The four paths are not included within the realms, as are the four fruits of asceticism and Nibbāna—
these phenomena are not included within the realms.
2.4.2.13.15. The Dyad of Leading Out (Niyyānikaduka).
Which phenomena lead out?
The four paths that are not included [within the mundane].
These phenomena lead to liberation.
Which phenomena do not lead to liberation?
Wholesome states in the three planes, unwholesome states, resultant states in the four planes, functional-inefficient states in the three planes, and form, as well as Nibbāna.
These phenomena are not leading to liberation.
2.4.2.13.16. The Pair on the Fixed:
Which phenomena are fixed?
The four types of consciousness associated with wrong view and the two types of consciousness accompanied by grief—
these states may be either fixed or unfixed.
The four supramundane paths are unfixed.
These states are fixed. Which states are unfixed?
The four types of consciousness-arising associated with greed but dissociated from views, and the consciousness-arising associated with doubt.
A state of consciousness accompanied by restlessness; wholesome states in the three planes; resultant states in the four planes;
functional-inindeterminate states in the three planes; and material form and Nibbāna—these phenomena are indeterminate.
2.4.2.13.17. With-Superior (Sauttara-duka).
Which phenomena are with-superior?
The wholesome in the three planes; the unwholesome; the resultants in the three planes; the functional-indeterminate in the three planes; and all form.
These phenomena are surpassable.
Which phenomena are unsurpassable?
The four paths not included within the mundane, the four fruits of recluseship, and Nibbāna.
These phenomena are unsurpassed.
2.4.2.13.18. The Pair on Having a Refuge:
Which phenomena have a refuge?
The twelve unwholesome types of consciousness—
these states are with conflict (saraṇa).
Which states are without conflict (araṇa)?
Wholesome states in the four planes, resultant states in the four planes, functional-undetermined states in the three planes, matter, and Nibbāna—
these phenomena are without conflict (*araṇā*).
The extraction of the meaning is finished.
The Dhammasaṅgaṇī treatise is completed.
